name: Galeazzi fracture-dislocation
aliases: distal radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption

reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: A fracture of the distal third of the radial shaft combined with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ)
Termed a fracture of necessity in adults because stable union and forearm function reliably require operative fixation
DRUJ instability may be subtle; clues include an associated ulnar styloid base fracture, DRUJ widening and altered ulnar variance
The counterpart injury is the Monteggia fracture-dislocation (proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation)
The usual mechanism is a fall on the outstretched hand with forearm rotation, or a direct blow
Treatment is anatomical plate fixation of the radius, after which the DRUJ is assessed and, if reduced and stable, immobilised in supination, or stabilised operatively if unstable
Radiographs must include the wrist and elbow to evaluate the whole forearm ring
reference.pathophysiology: The radius and ulna form a functional ring joined by the interosseous membrane and the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, so a shaft fracture rarely occurs in isolation. In the Galeazzi injury a force applied to the distal forearm fractures the distal radial shaft; the resulting radial shortening and angulation disrupt the distal radioulnar joint, tearing its stabilising ligaments or avulsing the ulnar styloid. If the radius is fixed without recognising and addressing the DRUJ, residual instability causes pain, weakness of grip and loss of forearm rotation.
additionalDifferentials: Essex-Lopresti injury involving the interosseous membrane and proximal radioulnar joint
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the forearm including the wrist and elbow
Assessment of DRUJ congruity, ulnar variance and the ulnar styloid
CT of the DRUJ with contralateral comparison when reduction is uncertain
Intra-operative stress testing of the DRUJ after radial fixation
MRI for triangular fibrocartilage complex injury in chronic or occult instability
redFlags: Unrecognised DRUJ instability leading to failure of treatment
Neurovascular compromise of the forearm or hand
reference.prognosis: With anatomical radial fixation and appropriate DRUJ stabilisation the outcome is generally good; a missed or untreated distal radioulnar joint injury causes chronic pain, weakness and restricted forearm rotation.
pitfalls: Fixing the radial fracture while overlooking distal radioulnar joint instability
Immobilising the forearm in the wrong rotation after reduction
Missing an associated ulnar styloid base fracture signalling DRUJ injury
Failing to image the whole forearm including the wrist
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Anatomical open reduction and internal plate fixation of the distal radial shaft, a fracture of necessity that requires operative fixation in adults
Intra-operative assessment and reduction of the distal radioulnar joint after radial fixation, immobilising in supination when it is reduced and stable
Operative stabilisation of the distal radioulnar joint by ligament repair or pinning if it remains unstable after radial fixation
Analgesia, initial immobilisation and careful neurovascular assessment of the limb
Structured hand therapy and graded rehabilitation to restore forearm rotation and grip strength after immobilisation
Radiographic follow-up to confirm union and detect recurrent distal radioulnar joint instability
Referral to orthopaedic or hand surgery for definitive operative management
